@graph.headline: Family Galápagos Cruises: Choosing a Ship That Works With Kids

mainEntity.name: What is the minimum age for a Galápagos cruise?

acceptedAnswer.text: It varies by vessel and operator — there's no single fleet-wide rule. Some ships welcome young children on any departure; others set a minimum age or restrict younger kids to family departures. We hold the current policy for each vessel, so ask us before you settle on a specific ship.

mainEntity.name: Do Galápagos cruises have family or connecting cabins?

acceptedAnswer.text: Many do — triple cabins and connecting or adjoining cabins are common — but the number and configuration differ by ship, and a small yacht may have just one or two. Availability moves fast in peak periods. Tell us your party size and we'll find current vessels whose cabins genuinely fit.

mainEntity.name: How much does a family Galápagos cruise cost?

acceptedAnswer.text: Our own fleet analysis puts cruises at roughly $445–$2,193 per person per day (median about $907). Multiply by every traveller and every night, then add the fixed per-person costs: the $200 park fee, about $20 transit card and about $400–$500 flights. Children usually pay a per-berth fare too.

mainEntity.name: Do children pay the Galápagos National Park fee and flights?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. The $200 park fee, about $20 INGALA transit card and about $400–$500 mainland flights all apply per person, children included, unless a specific reduced child rate is documented. Reduced park-fee rates do exist for children — ask us whether your chosen ship or the Park applies one for your family.

mainEntity.name: Are Galápagos cruises safe for kids?

acceptedAnswer.text: Galápagos travel is tightly regulated. A GNPS-certified naturalist guide leads every landing on a fixed schedule, with biosecurity checks and a rule to stay at least 2 metres from wildlife. Landings are by panga (Zodiac), wet or dry. Several ships carry a doctor on board — we'll tell you which.

mainEntity.name: What activities can children do on a Galápagos cruise?

acceptedAnswer.text: Snorkelling, kayaking, panga (Zodiac) rides and guided walks are the mainstays. But permitted activities depend on the visitor site under National Park rules — not every site allows every activity. Wet and dry landings are standard, so younger children may need a steadying hand ashore.

mainEntity.name: How many days should a family cruise be?

acceptedAnswer.text: Cruises run 4–15 days. All island regions are reachable on a 5-day-or-longer cruise; only Fernandina and west Isabela need that length. Shorter 4–6-day trips can suit younger children's attention spans, while 5–8 days gives teens more snorkel and kayak time.

mainEntity.name: Do we need an expensive ship to see the best islands with kids?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Nearly all vessels reach nearly all islands, so islands visited don't set the price tier or the quality. Choose on cabins, guide-to-guest ratio and activity fit instead. A higher star class doesn't reliably cost more or reach different islands.

mainEntity.name: Do solo parents or grandparents pay a single supplement?

acceptedAnswer.text: Single supplements vary by operator and departure — some are reduced or waived on select dates, others apply in full. There's no fleet-wide figure. Tell us your dates and party and we'll find the departures that don't penalise a single adult travelling with children.
